name: Nri

span.note: Founding dates range from the 9th to the 16th century.

summary.text: Nri was not a kingdom of conquest. Its priest-king, the Eze Nri, and his travelling agents cleansed abominations, crowned titled men and settled disputes across a large part of Igboland, a ritual authority without an army. The bronzes of Igbo-Ukwu, from about the 9th century, are linked to its early history. Its power faded in the 18th century, and the British ended it in 1911. Nri’s royal line descends from Eri, the founder of the Umueri towns. Prince M. C. M. Idigo of Aguleri (1955), and the colonial writers Meek (1937) and Boston (1960), recorded Eri as an Igala warrior who came down from Idah. Nri’s own tradition says he came down from the sky.

snapshots.title: Igbo-Ukwu and early Nri
snapshots.text: At Igbo-Ukwu, a burial of a titled man and a store of ritual bronzes, cast with great skill around the 9th century, show a wealthy ritual centre linked to long-distance trade.

snapshots.title: Ifikuanim and the ritual kingship
snapshots.text: After Eri, Ifikuanim becomes the first Eze Nri, perhaps around 1225. The Eze Nri is a priest-king with ritual, not military, power. He is chosen after an interregnum of at least seven years, while the dead king's signs are read, and is installed after a journey to Aguleri on the Anambra river, where he sits on Eri's throne, then returns to Nri for a symbolic burial and rising. Nri's agents, the ndi Nri, marked with ichi scars and carrying staffs of peace, travel to cleanse abominations; local men who buy the ozo and nze titles become mbùríchi, the Eze Nri's representatives.

snapshots.title: The height of Nri's ritual reach
snapshots.text: At its height, from the fourth to the ninth Eze Nri, Nri's ritual authority reaches about a quarter of Igboland and beyond: northern and central Igboland, Igbo towns west of the Niger and communities under Benin's sway. Allegiance comes by oath, not force; anyone carrying the omu palm frond travels safe. The peace Nri keeps lets trade flourish: horses and seashells appear in its bronzes and ivory in its burials.

snapshots.note: Ritual reach is not rule. The zone shows where Nri agents worked, as described by Onwuejeogwu; its edges are uncertain.

snapshots.title: A sanctuary for the enslaved
snapshots.text: From the reign of the tenth Eze Nri any slave who sets foot on Nri soil is free, and Nri holds no slaves itself. At the Igu Aro festival, the counting of the year, Nri's communities send tribute and receive yam medicine and blessings; violence is held to pollute the earth, and the Eze Nri's weapon is ritual exclusion. But from the tenth to the fourteenth reigns quarrels grow, probably fed by the slave trade around Nri.

links.label: Igu Aro: communities bring tribute at the year's counting

snapshots.title: Decline
snapshots.text: The slave trade, the Aro network and pressure from Igala and Benin weaken Nri's ritual authority.

snapshots.title: The British end Nri's power
snapshots.text: From 1905 to 1911 the British clash with Nri, and in 1911 a colonial expedition forces the reigning Eze Nri to renounce the ritual power of the ikenga. Nineteen Eze Nri are recorded that year. The title survives as a traditional throne, revived since 1974.

today.text: The Eze Nri still reigns at Agukwu Nri, Anaocha LGA, Anambra State, as a traditional ruler.
today.title: Eze Nri

reviewNotes: The Nri reach is drawn as a ritual zone, not a territory.

Eri’s origin is contested. The Igala origin follows Idigo (1955), as the owner asked on 2026-10-07; the sky origin is Nri’s own tradition. Both are kept, and the event "Eri comes down from Igala" is marked disputed.
